speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Singapore has consistently been ranked as one of the safest countries in the world.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: People feel safe walking alone at night, violent crimes involving weapons are few and far between; and attacks involving guns and explosives are extremely rare.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Our highly safe and secure environment is, in large part, attributable to the stringent laws that we have in place to regulate dangerous activities involving articles such as guns, explosives and other weapons, and the criminalising of unlawful actions involving these items.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Arms and Explosives Act or AEA, in short, is the primary Act for regulating the handling of guns, explosives, explosive precursors, certain other weapons like swords, daggers and spears, and noxious substances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For simplicity, I shall refer to these items collectively henceforth as "GEW" – Guns, Explosives, Weapons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In addition, for drafting reasons, from here on, by "weapons", I shall be referring only to those weapons scheduled in the AEA or the Bill like swords, spears and daggers, and not guns or explosives which I shall treat as separate items.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Four other Acts, namely, the Arms Offences Act, Explosives Substances Act, Corrosive and Explosives Substances and Offensive Weapons Act, and Dangerous Fireworks Act, also deal with GEW-related crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We cannot take our safety and security situation for granted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, the threat of an extremist attack remains very real.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There have been serious incidents in countries with strict gun and weapon laws.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Many of these incidents were not carried out by military organisations or state-sponsored activists, but individuals with extremist views and sentiments, using guns or knives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Among others, the series of religiously-motivated terrorist attacks and the beheading of a school teacher in France late last year as well as the Christchurch mass shootings in 2019 by a gunman, where 51 individuals lost their lives and 40 were injured.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We must not presume that these attacks cannot happen here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Recently, 37 individuals were investigated by ISD and the Police for inciting violence, stoking communal unrest and making derogatory remarks against Muslims.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: One of them was eventually arrested under the Internal Security Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: He had bought foldable knives in Singapore, which he claimed he would use for attacks against Hindus in Bangladesh.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, technology is posing an increasing challenge to effective enforcement against GEW-related crimes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Internet has significantly facilitated the trafficking and manufacture of GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: One can easily get online and access materials and instructions to manufacture GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There are lethal forms of GEW that can be purchased over the Internet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Third, we need to optimise our enforcement resources to better regulate a growing industry.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The AEA was last amended in 2007 to introduce regulation for explosive precursors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Every licence requires resources to vet the licensee and to conduct inspections.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Police, who are currently the regulators under the AEA, need to be able to regulate this growing pool of licensees effectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Otherwise, there is a risk of lapses going undetected, potentially resulting in disastrous safety or security consequences, such as the recent explosion that happened in Beirut which killed more than 200 people.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill reinforces the Government's position that any handling of GEW is a privilege that is conditioned on the overriding need to ensure that we meet the objective of public safety and security, and that strict controls are required to achieve this objective.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In particular, the Bill will strive to achieve two objectives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, to strengthen our levers to promote safe and secure GEW handling and further minimise the risks posed by GEW, and second, to ensure a more calibrated and coherent enforcement framework for these items.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We have, in the process, consulted industry stakeholders to explain the amendments and also obtained their feedback.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: We intend to achieve our first objective of strengthening levers to promote safe, secure and responsible GEW handling and further minimise the risks posed by GEW in two ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, by further tightening controls over high-risk GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, the maximum fines for unlicensed activities involving explosive precursors (EPs) are $100,000 for entities and $50,000 for individuals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, the maximum fine for arms and explosives is only $10,000, even though the degree of harm that can be caused is comparable to that of EPs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In addition, the Bill allows the Minister for Home Affairs to prescribe items as prohibited GEW, offences related to which will attract even higher fines of up to $100,000 for persons and $200,000 for entities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: These are items which are identified as particularly dangerous or may be more readily concealed and would be particularly suited to unlawful use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, certain types of automatic gun commonly used by terrorists, which are highly dangerous and clearly have no legitimate use.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: No licence will be granted for the handling of these items.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, the Bill criminalises the unauthorised possession of digital blueprints of guns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, a person could easily find on the Internet, materials for gun making and manufacture a fully workable gun using a 3D printer and a gun blueprint taken from the Internet.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: As a case in point, in 2019, a shooter in Germany had brought along guns with components that were manufactured using 3D printing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Those guns were eventually not used in carrying out the attacks, but were his back-up arsenal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In this context, "possession" includes the scenario where a person in Singapore physically possesses a storage device containing such a blueprint, as well as the scenario where a person in Singapore stores a blueprint outside Singapore, such as in an overseas cloud storage device.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To be clear, the intent is not to target persons who genuinely have no knowledge and could not reasonably be expected to have known, that he or she possessed the digital blueprint for making a gun.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, a person who merely browses out of curiosity and finds on the Internet a gun blueprint, and the blueprint is only temporarily stored in the browser cache.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, we have the threat posed by drones laden with GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In 2018, explosives-laden drones were used during an attack on Nicolas Maduro, the Venezuela President, when he was making a public speech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Several members of the Bolivarian National Guard were injured.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: GEW-laden drones can circumvent conventional physical security measures, such as physical fences and CCTVs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill reinforces the 2015 amendment to the Air Navigation Act, which makes it an offence if a person operates an unmanned aircraft and the unmanned aircraft carries a prohibited item, which can be any weapon.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill also introduces powers for the Licensing Officers to authorise third parties to do low-risk compliance checks, to allow the regulator to focus on high-risk GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, all licensing compliance checks are performed by Police officers regardless of the risk posed by the GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There is scope to use our limited Police resources more optimally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Our intent is to delegate checks on low-risk items, such as weapons and air guns, to qualified persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 80 therefore allows the Licensing Officer or LO in short, with the approval of the Minister for Home Affairs, to appoint Compliance Officers to exercise certain powers of the LO, such as the powers of inspection.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, while the vast majority of the GEW industry are compliant, we continue to encounter episodes of lapse among licensees.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Some happened because the licensees wanted to save costs, or wanted to make compliance more convenient for themselves.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In so doing, they compromised safety and security.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Any lapse or breach involving GEW can result in catastrophic consequences.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: MHA has identified areas where we can further improve compliance and enhance regulatory effectiveness.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, the Bill requires specific periodic reporting of GEWs by licensees and allows for inspections by regulators.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There are risks to the community when guns, explosives or lethal weapons are not accounted for.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 59, 60 and 61 require licensees to update the Licensing Officer on changes to their management and to periodically report on their conduct of the regulated activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clauses 70 to 72 grant the Licensing Officer and authorised officers additional powers, such as the powers of inspection and powers to order the production of documents, to determine whether information given to the regulators is correct or whether regulatory action needs to be taken.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, the Bill expands the scope of regulation to cover GEW-related activities and items more comprehensively, in a calibrated manner.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In particular, the Bill introduces a class licensing regime for low or moderate-risk users and activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, the AEA requires all persons conducting GEW-related activities to be either individually licensed, or to be exempted, which means they will fall outside the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But there are certain low or moderate-risk GEW-related activities which warrant some regulatory control, just not to the extent of individual licensing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Under these clauses, a person who meets certain criteria, which will be set out in subsidiary legislation, such as being a member of a school air gun club, is automatically treated as licensed and allowed to carry out a GEW regulated activity, subject to the conditions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: With class licensing, the person need not be put through security clearance and need not apply or renew for individual licence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To elaborate, public interest grounds include considerations relating to public order as well as public security and safety.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, if an air gun class licensee is found to be a gang member, Police can then disapply this person from continuing to handle GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Next, the Bill also revises our regulatory approach towards weapons and gun accessories.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, "arms", as defined under the AEA, covers guns and major gun parts and five specified weapons, that is, swords, bayonets, daggers, spears and spearheads.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, the controls and penalties are not calibrated according to the risk posed by the item.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The specified weapons pose lower risks than guns and major gun parts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: But the way “arms” is defined now, means that these lower-risk items require the same controls, and offences involving these items carry the same penalties as offences involving guns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, other weapons which may pose equal or higher risk as the five specified weapons, such as machetes, are not regulated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Our policy intent is to have a regime that comprehensively controls GEW, and in a manner which is commensurate with their risk.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The expanded list of specified weapons to be regulated is reflected in the First Schedule, and will include other dangerous weapons like throwing stars and knuckledusters, which are very unlikely to have common day-to-day uses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In addition, the Bill expands the scope of regulation to cover gun accessories, such as flash suppressors and silencers, which can be used to enhance the performance of guns.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, the penalties for gun accessories are lower than those for guns as they pose a lower risk.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill also allows shooting range operations to be regulated, to ensure safety at the range.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Today, operating a shooting range is not an activity that needs to be licensed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, we want to be able to ensure that safety and security measures at shooting ranges are adequate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, the Licensing Officer may need to impose requirements for the deployment of a range safety officer or installation of robust perimeter fencing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 19 therefore makes it an offence to operate a shooting range or paintball range without a licence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill also confers on the Licensing Officer, or LO, greater operational flexibility, to act swiftly where necessary to deal with new dangers or where there are increased risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: First, the LO may change the licensing conditions during the tenure of the licence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Clause 54 allows the LO to add, delete or modify conditions during the tenure of a licence, subject to due process.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Second, there will be a new power for the Minister for Home Affairs to issue security directions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Sometimes, a security situation requires a more expedient response than what modifying licensing conditions allows, given the need to provide for due process when licensing conditions are changed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: If there is imminent threat to life or property, for instance, clause 64 allows the Minister to direct licensees, class licensees and even exempted persons to immediately put in place enhanced measures, or temporarily suspend, cease or scale down their activities for a period of time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: It is non-appealable and is time-limited to six months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The other key objective of this Bill is to ensure a more calibrated and coherent enforcement framework for GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In developing this Bill, we took the opportunity to rationalise the offences and penalties across the various GEW-related laws to achieve greater coherence, consistency and clarity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: There are currently some inconsistencies in penalties for offences with similar offence elements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, section 3 of the Arms Offences Act, or AOA, criminalises unlawful possession of arms or ammunition and the penalties include caning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Section 13 of the AEA similarly criminalises unlicensed possession of arms, but the penalties are lighter and they do not include caning.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In addition, certain offences have similar penalties, even though the egregiousness of the offences differ.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, under the AEA, the offence of conducting an activity without a licence attracts similar penalties as a breach of licensing conditions, even though the latter is considered less severe.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To this end, clauses 93 and 94 amend the AOA and the Corrosive and Explosives Substances and Offensive Weapons Act, or CESOWA, in short, to clarify that offences made out under these Acts involve criminal intent and therefore attract heavier punishments and penalties, thus distinguishing them from offences under the AEA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Even as penalties are being raised, the penalties are also calibrated to match the egregiousness of the offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, the penalty for the offence of unlicensed possession of explosives for individuals is higher than that for breach of licensing conditions involving explosives, as the former is considered more egregious.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This is a fairer approach, to ensure that the penalties are proportional to the offence, while maintaining our tough stance against misuse of GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill also streamlines the regulatory approach for dangerous fireworks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Currently, dangerous fireworks are prohibited under the Dangerous Fireworks Act, or DFA.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: However, fireworks are explosives as well, and ought to be regulated as such under a single law.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: All activities involving fireworks including discharge, transportation and storage will be regulated as explosives under this Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Last but not least, the Bill contains provisions that put on firmer footing some existing practices which remain relevant in our new security environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: Screening requirements, which serve to mitigate the risks associated with GEW, are presently imposed through the "fit and proper" criteria for licensees, or mandated through the licensing conditions for the workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: This has shortcomings as there is no consistency and direct link between the validity of security clearances and the authorisation to engage in the regulated activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: To lend greater clarity to the industry, clauses 41 to 46 set out the security clearance process and considerations for granting, suspending or revoking the security clearance of an individual.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: For example, the individual’s physical or mental health and participation in criminal activity are material factors in screening.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: The Bill will also make clear the obligations of the licensee and the worker.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: At the same time, a special worker of a licensee, who handles GEW knowingly, or with reckless disregard, that his or her security clearance is not valid, will be committing an offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: I cannot emphasise enough that the safety and security that we currently enjoy in Singapore should never be taken for granted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan) (for the Minister for Home Affairs)
text: In this regard, the Bill seeks to ensure that our regulatory framework remains robust to deter and prevent the misuse and mishandling of GEW, which can have very serious consequences for our safety and security, while respecting the need to allow legitimate uses for some GEW.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This is a timely move given the increasing rate of technological advancement of additive manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would also like to ask if there would be any circumstances that a person or an organisation would be authorised to possess a 3D blueprint of a gun, and what would be the obligations placed on such a person or organisation to ensure that there are proper safeguards to prevent misuse of such blueprints.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I would, therefore, urge that we start to think about how we should regulate specific types of 3D printers that are able to manufacture these guns.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As the Executive Secretary of the United Workers of Electronics & Electrical Industries, I have seen first-hand how 3D printers have become more versatile today, and are now able to print different materials, alloys and even carbon fibre.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There are several types of 3D printers currently available on the market, catering to a wide range of customers – from action figure enthusiasts, to start-ups doing rapid prototyping, to aeroplane manufacturers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: These 3D printers can use a wide variety of “raw ingredients”, from plastics, to metal, to carbon fibre.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Examples would include the Stereolithography printer, the Direct Metal Laser Sintering printer, and the Electron Beam Melting printer.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As the Minister of State mentioned in his speech yesterday, drones loaded with weapons can pose a serious threat to safety and security.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As early as 2015, there were news reports of a teenager in the United States who had already figured out a way to mount a handgun onto a drone and fire it remotely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To make things more worrying, instructional videos on how to do this, which is to replicate this remote firing process, can easily be found online.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As technology progresses and the effective range for drones increases exponentially, it is likely that drones can be controlled beyond an operator’s visual line of sight, and foreign sources can use their drones to enter our airspace with malicious intent.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many Members of this House would recall the drone disruptions that happened at Changi Airport in June 2019, which shows that malicious actors need not necessarily load a drone with a weapon to cause damage in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to the Minister of State, this is to allow our Licensing Officers to focus their attention on high-risk GEWs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While gun replicas are harmless on its own, the high resemblance to real guns can cause a lot of undue fear and alarm, especially to vulnerable people such as the elderly and children.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Many replica gun hobbyists are deeply private and most pursue their passion quietly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, just as 3D printing technology gives criminals the ability to produce their own guns, it would also allow these hobbyists to 3D-print their own gun replicas.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Are there any plans to engage gun replica hobbyists, so that we can allow them some flexibility in pursuing their passion within a safeguarded space, perhaps, through a proper licensing framework?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, the introduction of the Bill is timely as it will allow our enforcement agencies to keep pace with criminals seeking to use new technologies to commit crime and perform acts of terror in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While it is important to ban the unauthorised possession of 3D gun blueprints, we need to also prevent the downloading of these blueprints on the Dark Web and regulate specific 3D printers that can use these blueprints to produce a functional gun.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As we move into the new decade, drones and other unmanned aerial vehicles will increasingly become a security threat, and we will need to step up on our anti-drone capabilities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I also hope that the Ministry could do more to engage hobbyists, who often keep their hobbies in the dark, for fear of running afoul of the law, as they, too, can use the same additive manufacturing technology to 3D-print replica guns, and even functional ones.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also agree that there is a need to update the legislation to keep up with new technology and threats.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party endorses the strict stance of weapons control and I am in general support of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 43 of the Bill provides that licences may be issued to individuals as well as non-individuals, such as corporate entities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For individuals' licence to possess firearms, I believe there was a historical practice where wealthy individuals and/or their security personnel were permitted to carry firearms for protection.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was because they were considered to be at risk of being kidnapped for ransom.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for licences issued to organisations, clause 43 states that security clearances must first be obtained for all individuals who are responsible executives as well as at least one close associate of the entity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While it is quite logical that responsible executives, such as the CEO, president or general manager, would need security clearances, the additional requirement for the close associates to also have security clearance needs further explanation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A close associate of an entity is defined as a person who either holds 5% of equity or voting rights or is a person who will be managing the business.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why is it necessary to have security clearance for a 5% shareholder who may not be participating in managing the business?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And, if it deemed relevant to clear shareholders, why is the bar set at only 5%, meaning that the remaining 95% of shareholders do not need security clearance?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is this meant to cater for companies whose shareholders are mainly corporations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to the factors considered by the Licensing Officer in deciding on security clearances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is stated in clause 45 that the Licensing Officer must consider various factors, including whether the applicant has participated in any criminal activity, has a history of violence or threat of violence and whether clearing the applicant is contrary to the public interest or national security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The explicit listing of the factors is welcome for transparency.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At this juncture, it would be useful for the Ministry to clarify whether the Licensing Officer still has discretion to grant the security clearance to an applicant who fails on one or some criteria, say, the applicant has an old conviction in the Youth Court when he was a teenager.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another question on security clearances is how the Licensing Officer would access information submitted to him in such applications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 45(2) provides that to assist the Licensing Officer, the Commissioner of Police or a law enforcement agency may provide a report to him to help assess applications for security clearances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, the Licensing Officer can verify whether the applicant is known to have participated in criminal or violent acts and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, I believe the Ministry expects to receive applications from foreigners, such as those who need short-term licences for trade fairs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will be Licensing Officer verify the background information of foreign applicants?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I hope there will be no compromise in ensuring that foreign persons are subject to the same standard of checks as resident applicants.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 80 of the Bill provides that the Licensing Officer can appoint an individual who is not a public officer to be a compliance officer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the Ministry’s press release of 3 November, the investigation and enforcement of breaches will still be handled by Police officers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also note some restrictions on the powers of a Compliance Officer under clause 80(7).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, under Part 6 of the Bill, compliance officers will be empowered to check licensees for compliance including inspection of premises, asking for information and explanations, stopping vehicles in transit and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These are potentially confrontational situations at locations where guns and weapons are kept.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Upon further reading and consideration, I am convinced that we need to do so.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Our environment has changed and technology has evolved tremendously.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Updating our legislation to take into account the advent of technology is timely, and a constant reminder to ourselves to keep up with changes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: While we welcome and embrace the benefits of new technology such as 3D printing, we need to guard against the pitfalls it can bring.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: With today's technology, manufacturers could produce toy guns almost as good and functional as the real guns, which can pose a genuine threat to our lives too.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Hence, there is also a need to protect our people against such threats.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Security and safety must remain top priorities for our nation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We are fortunate to be able to provide a fairly secure environment for Singaporeans and residents so far.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Even so, there are still cases of violence and unauthorised use of fireworks.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Our tight control over guns and weapons has helped minimised the destructive impact of such events.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: However, we must not take things for granted.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: It is of the utmost importance that we continue to remain vigilant and stringent on security measures.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: There have been many incidents and tragedies in countries that had legalised arms possession.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We must continue to have zero tolerance towards guns and weapons, just as we do not tolerate drugs in our jurisdiction.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We must continue to send a strong signal to all in Singapore and to others beyond our shores that we have zero tolerance for any action that could threaten our peace and security.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: In addition, we need to tighten the surveillance of potential influence and threats in social media.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We will need the support and technical expertise of social media service providers to help us defend against perpetrators who use social media to advance their interests and promote the use of violence and weapons of mass disruption in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Last but not least, it is important that we continue to promote tolerance and acceptance among our multiracial, multilingual, multi-cultural and multi-religious community members.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Religious and racial harmony must always be our core value.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the key objective of the Act is to consolidate a number of older pieces of legislation, it also introduces a number of updates that are designed to accommodate the reality of weapons in the modern world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Historically, our ability to successfully control the distribution of weapons was premised on the combination of managing supply and demand.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On the supply side, we have been able to tightly control the inflow of goods and people due to our small, island geography and sophisticated policing of porous points along our borders.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In terms of demand, we have instituted some of the world's most severe gun control laws – with punishments for unlawful possession, trafficking and use stipulated in the Arms Offences Act of 1973 and 2008, and Arms and Explosives Act of 1913 and 2013.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We have supported these sticks with the carrot of an efficient, uncorrupt Police force.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This largely airtight control is now being undermined by the advancement of technology.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The ease of obtaining, securing and subsequently deleting electronic blueprints for weapons means that for a digitally-sophisticated population such as ours, the ability to independently print guns, if one chooses to do so, will increasingly be trivial.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, if printed with non-standard materials, such 3D- printed guns will become increasingly undetectable with our usual screening devices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Still, it appears only to be a matter of when, not if, technology catches up.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The basic principles of deterrence are straightforward and, I am certain, well understood by Members of this House.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: An individual with the proclivity to exercise violence may choose not to do so, if he or she believes that there will be a credible threat of a possibly disproportionately large retaliatory response.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Termed "mutually assured destruction", this threat of a response was what characterised the Cold War and what kept the United States and Soviet Union from pursuing outright war, with most conflicts pursued by proxy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Same arguments are often made in the context of defenders of the right of individuals to carry weapons in self-defence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now, the problem with this simple logic of deterrence, and the reason why strict weapons control is generally preferable, is that the deterrent effect is no longer applicable when we relax some of these basic assumptions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In particular, brandishing a gun on an unsuspecting victim confers first-mover advantage to the aggressor, which nullifies the threat of a retaliatory response.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A gun in one's backpack is of no use if an erstwhile robber has one pointed at your face.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And the simple rationality that undergirds deterrence theory also breaks down when one agent is viewed as particularly susceptible to emotional response.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is, for example, why some observers have argued that dealing with North Korea may require actions beyond simple deterrence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the majority of the subsequent clauses, such as clauses 17 or 20 or 27, prescribe penalties for violations; relying, as it were, on the stick rather than the carrot.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: My argument is that we need to be more creative about our use of deterrence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The crux of the matter is this: We should be willing to consider the efficacy of a blunt reliance on strict weapons control as our central tool for containing violent crime and take efforts to address the underlying motivations for crime more seriously.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, crime is a complex and multi-faceted phenomenon.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Criminologists point to factors as varied as the thermal climate, urban density, inhabitant characteristics and psycho-social risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But two important drivers have emerged recently and stressed the effects of poverty and income inequality.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Of course, I am not suggesting that the Government has not made any efforts at addressing these more fundamental drivers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What we should not forget though is that an important spillover of our policies to diminish inequality and eliminate poverty is that we yield the payoff of reduced crime too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: On that note of general caution, I assert my support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I applaud the effort to keep legislation concerning guns, explosives and weapons – referred to as GEW by Minister of State Desmond Tan – updated especially given the fact that advancements in technology and open borders have made it significantly easier to procure and manufacture GEWs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We in Singapore are fortunate that our law enforcement agencies and supportive citizenry has kept our nation safe and free from the proliferation of GEWs.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we must not rest upon our laurels in the face of recent developments. 3D printing is certainly an exciting and revolutionary technology as the designs you can manufacture now are effectively limited only by your imagination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As someone who is exposed to 3D printing at the workplace, I can assure that whatever that you can think of, it is highly likely that the 3D printer can print it out for you. 3D printing is also relatively cheap compared to traditional manufacturing with lathes and milling machines.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These 3D printers can print many different kinds of materials – from plastics to carbon fibre reinforced thermoplastics, to even different metals for the more complex and sophisticated machines.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the industry, the use of 3D printing – or what is known as additive manufacturing or AM – is becoming more prevalent.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: AM has revolutionised how we design and manufacture components where there is little or even zero waste, unlike traditional subtractive manufacturing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: AM is forcing us to rethink supply chain and manufacturing strategies because now, anyone in any part of the world can manufacture a 3D component if he has the design and a 3D printer capable of doing it.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, there is also a lot of online resources available for free.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, there is an increasingly worrying global trend on the irresponsible use of 3D printing guns and offensive weapons.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One of my residents even showed me the design of a "Gutbuster" – a knuckleduster integrated with a dagger and a revolver.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is indeed a worrying trend given our objective of becoming a digitally connected nation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is also a strong online community of advocates pushing for the digital design of guns to be made available to all for free as an extension of the United States' second amendment on the freedom to bear arms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As an example, Cody Wilson, described as a crypto-anarchist, had designed and successfully tested his first 3D-printed gun, which he named "The Liberator".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He proceeded to upload it online for others to access for free.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A quick Google search also shows many examples of organisations distributing blueprints for guns and weapons with the intent of arming civilians to protect themselves and rise up against authorities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To further complicate these worrying trends, 3D printed guns are unserialised and therefore untraceable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They can also be made using plastics, making them undetectable by metal detectors at security points such as in our airports and other sensitive installations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: All these lead to the simple fact that there are low barriers of entry for anyone who has the interest to 3D print a gun or weapon.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Low printer cost, free downloadable software and blueprints open the gates to the proliferation of these 3D printed guns and other offensive weapons.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just some examples of the designs of guns that are available online: flying swallow revolver, zig-zag gun, AR15, FGC-9.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some are revolvers and some are semi-auto weapons.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Any person with very modest means and a broadband connection can effectively print his own gun in the comfort and privacy of his own homes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In fact, there are many YouTube videos that show just this.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The situation becomes increasingly dangerous when we take into consideration the instances of self-radicalised individuals on our shores.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Easy access to such technology seems like the perfect opportunity for a lone-wolf operative aiming to commit acts of terrorism.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is therefore imperative that we pass this Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to keep up with the advancements in 3D printing technology and deal with the low barriers to access blueprints, especially in the current global and societal context.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Like it or not, 3D printing of guns and other weapons is here with us and when it is misused, presents a clear and present danger to the safety and security of the general public.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given its importance, I would like to suggest the following considerations.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, I suggest that it should also consider gun modifications and attachments that can be used with malicious intent such as silencers, scopes and so on.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also note that digital blueprints for offensive weapons such as knuckledusters and daggers are not covered.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As someone who is excited about the benefits of 3D printing, I do understand that we do not want to stifle creativity and innovation and we also do not want to over-criminalise 3D printing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, how do we keep to the spirit of the law and prevent such offensive weapons from being used in our country?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Of the hundreds of thousands of parcels crossing our borders, I am glad and I am thankful that our Singapore Customs have the capability to detect, intercept and prevent such offensive weapons from crossing our borders.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we continue with this intent in this new world where we are unable to rely solely on the control at our physical borders to prevent these offensive weapons from appearing on our shores?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we get people to practice responsible 3D printing without over-criminalising it?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Since it is impractical to prevent people from having the blueprint of non gun-based weapons, at least, this will force those that are responsible for 3D printing to think twice on the use of 3D printed items, especially if it is used to cause harm in our society.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On enforcement, I would like to understand how MHA intends to enforce the unauthorised possession of the digital blueprints of guns.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we explore the banning of websites that advocate gun blueprint sharing?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can MHA make non-intrusive checks on residents to ensure that they do not have gun designs stored on their hard drives?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we have the right resource, skillset and organisational capability in MHA to tackle this threat?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe the community also has a wider role to play too.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we co-opt the community to understand the urgency of this issue and the threat that it poses to public security and safety?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can we educate the public to be vigilant and be on the lookout?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Is there a role family members should play, especially in our objective to identify early radicalised individuals who may turn out to be lone-wolf operatives?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we provide safe, anonymous whistle-blowing channels for the public or family members?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we also ensure that the ease of access to 3D printers in schools and other agencies are not abused?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is great that many of our kids are exposed to 3D printers in schools nowadays.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, anyone with computer aided design skills – which is now taught in schools – is able to design a simple, sharp-ended knuckleduster and have it printed in hours.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They do not even need to wait for weeks for shipment from overseas.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another consideration is on the declaration and serialisation of some highly sophisticated 3D printers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would help to monitor its use and ensure it is not in the hands of individuals with ill intent and forces the 3D printing contract manufacturers to be aware of the downstream usage of their manufactured products.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, while we protect ourselves internally from the possession and manufacture of 3D printed guns, how do we protect our borders from the importation of 3D printed guns or weapons, especially those made from thermoplastics that can escape metal detection at our borders?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The dangers of not detecting such guns and weapons cannot be underestimated.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):    The advancements in 3D printing technology present us with exciting and promising new opportunities. 3D printing technology is transforming the manufacturing world and forcing us to rethink supply chain strategies. 3D printing is capable of creating any product that can be made anywhere in the world.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The usage of 3D printing is now growing.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It augments and sometimes replaces traditional manufacturing processes such as "lathe" and "milling machines".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, it is important for our people to explore, understand and possess the competence in this technology that is increasingly becoming the norm in the new economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Last month, the M3@Pasir-Ris Punggol organized a 3D printing course.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The course was held for people of all ages; young and old.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The course participants were able to learn about 3D printing, and they were excited about the potential of this technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although 3D printing brings a lot of benefits, we also need to be aware of the threats posed by this technology.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As 3D printing technology and weapon blueprints are readily available online, coupled with the negative online elements that promote terrorism, there are individuals who have started to produce weapons using 3D printing in their own homes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, we need to be vigilant towards those who may be using them with dangerous intentions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As concerned members of the community and family members, we need to know the tell-tale signs of such individuals and contact the authorities so that Singapore continues to be safe and secure.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Twenty-twenty had been a particularly difficult year for all.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition to the COVID-19 health crisis, many parts of the world also experienced political turmoil and upheavals in their streets.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is necessary with the rapid advancement of 3D printing technology, which has been improving by leaps and bounds.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is frightening and sobering to see how the Internet has enabled the world to connect and share all good and bad.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Information and videos on how to make and assemble many items are shared freely or for a fee on the web.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We have to be especially wary of digital printers being used to make guns, weapons and explosives that could be assembled in installments and shipped here without anyone knowing their purpose.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These could be shipped in different batches and assembled here.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would the Minister share how we can counter this threat?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is there a guide being drawn up to help enforcement officers identify and keep a lookout for items that could be suspicious as they would be used to assemble illegal items?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):    We have to be especially wary of digital printers being used to make guns, weapons and explosives that could be assembled in installments and shipped here, without anyone knowing their purpose.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A concern I have is how the Singapore Police Force is going to spot and identify gun or weapon parts which can be imported into Singapore in hard-to-detect bits and pieces, deceptively mis-labelled as something else.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These could be shipped in different batches and assembled here.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will the Minister share how we can counter this threat?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Is there a guide being drawn up to help enforcement officers identify and keep a look-out for items that could be suspicious as they would be used to assemble illegal items?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have four clarifications to raise on this Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first clarification is on the proposed definition of “store” and the four limbs of the definition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The definition first sets out the first and second limbs, followed by the phrase “and includes”, then the third and fourth limbs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if this should be interpreted to mean that the first and second limbs are broad definitions, and the third and fourth limbs are specific examples of the first and second limbs?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also clarify if the third and fourth limbs are examples and do not exhaustively set out situations where a gun or major part of a gun is deemed to be stored?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I seek this clarification because the third limb refers very specifically to being in possession of any explosive or explosive precursor for more than 24 hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the definition of "weapon".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill defines weapon in the First Schedule, which comprises a detailed list, such as arrows, knives and swords.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The First Schedule does not provide any exceptions for imitation, replica or ornamental weapons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: By contrast, the definition of gun or explosives in the Bill does provide exceptions for imitation guns and explosives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, under section 13(6) of the existing Arms and Explosives Act, a licence is not required to possess a sword or dagger kept in a dwelling for ornamental purposes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While clause 94 of the Bill deems ornamental or theatrical weapons as lawful purpose for possessing an offensive weapon under the Corrosive and Explosive Substances and Offensive Weapons Act, it is not clear how imitation, replica or ornamental weapons are treated under the new Guns, Explosives and Weapons Control Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify if the term “weapon” is intended to cover imitation, replica or ornamental weapons?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If so, can the Minister share how it intends to address the enforcement issues that may arise because of the over-inclusiveness?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Ministry consider, for instance, issuing class licences for activities involving objects that fall within the definition of weapons but would not ordinarily be used to cause harm, such as imitation, replica or ornamental weapons?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is about variation orders for class licences.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 57(1) of the Bill allows the Minister to vary a class licence by order in the Gazette.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the Gazette is not necessarily accessible to the layperson.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To propose to vary a class licence, the Minister is required to publish a notice on a website or in other forms readily accessible to the public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the proposal to vary a class licence must be published, the order to vary itself is not subject to these requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For consistency and transparency, will MHA ensure that the variation order itself be published in forms readily accessible to the public?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My fourth and final point is about the enforcement powers of compliance officers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Despite not being public agents, compliance officers may exercise a range of enforcement powers under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify how compliance officers will be supervised in the exercise of these powers?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Having had the experience of being a former National Service Police Commander, I can see that this Bill has taken a holistic approach.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Not only has it appropriately increased the deterrence for offences with the intent to cause harm, it has also included proactive features in two key areas, namely: one, upstream preventive measures; and, two, the use of class licensing regime.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: These steps allow for better risk management without increased regulatory burden, of which, I have a request and one clarification for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Relating to the first point, a few years back, I previously practised at the National Shooting Centre at Choa Chu Kang under the oversight of a coach.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: At that time, I noticed that the procedures of the range were not as tight as now.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This measure is more reassuring for all range users as well as the public.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, in view of the tightened level of security and licensing requirements, I hope that the Ministry will keep the inconvenience to impacted stakeholders to a reasonable level in terms of, for example, wait time for licence registration and approvals, lead time for range and arms booking, as well as keeping the associated costs manageable.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: On the second point, the Bill’s calibration is evident by the inclusion of the new class licensing regime.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This class of licensing will facilitate the development of Shooting sports which is an area where Singapore has done well, with world-class athletes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In this way, class licensing will facilitate legitimate users and stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In concluding, Mr Speaker, Sir, this Bill is holistic in its approach and balanced.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is this appetite for and dedication to innovation that has put us on the map for seven consecutive years as the Asia Pacific’s most innovative nation, according to the Global Innovation Index.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Imagine, Mr Speaker, Sir, being able to speak into existence virtually any object the mind can conceive.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is the enormous potential of the innovative technology we know as 3D printing.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It has birthed communities fascinated by 3D printing’s ability to unleash their creativity with endless practical applications.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other than formal settings, such as professional manufacturers and designers or even academic institutions, 3D printing has found a place at the heart of several interest groups that tap on its versatility.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Those passionate about drones, e-scooters, Nerf, Warhammers, even baking, and so many more, have found 3D printing to add incredible value to their hobbies and passions.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond its obvious economic benefits and industrial uses, 3D printing has also been an added catalyst for hobbyists resourceful enough to tap on it.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, the Nerf community in Singapore, they have been around for many years, and this, traditionally, has been a competitive game involving the use of foam-based weaponry fired from primarily foam-based blasters.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hobbyists seek out and improvise their own arenas of play in parks or other spaces, where games are hosted and played by those within the Nerf community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Those who participate find this an exciting way to keep active and creative.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The technology allows hobbyists to forge more powerful blasters that greatly enhance their game.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Also, modifications to the aesthetics and performance of blasters are shared among the community to encourage innovation and celebrate each other’s achievements.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Government spends years and pours loads of resources for Singaporeans to pick up new technologies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But here we have a community that has eagerly adopted the exciting technology of 3D printing as an integral part of their interest.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More than that, I am heartened by the community spirit they display in wanting to be responsible citizens as well.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, modifications to blasters’ aesthetics that paint them black are frowned upon, as such realism might cause panic to the public.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hobbyists actively and responsibly refrain from such realism so as not to put the wider Nerf community’s interests at risk.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And that is, indeed, thoughtful of the community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The 3D printing community has also come under the spotlight for good reason during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is easy to be afraid of the unknown, as with exciting new technologies such as 3D printing.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So often, in the face of uncertainty and "what if's", our first foot out the door is to come down hard with regulation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When I consulted those in the 3D printing scene, from researchers, inventors to hobbyists, I found that many felt that the idea that one with malicious intent would resort to using home-based 3D printing to produce dangerous weapons such as guns would be a pretty distant one.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many pointed to lower hanging fruit such as pipe guns, given the impracticality of using a household-appropriate 3D printer to print functional weapons.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not only would important aspects of a functional weapon, such as ammunition, be impossible to forge using such 3D printers, 3D printed weapons themselves – according to the experts – would be unable to withstand the pressure of firing a bullet due to the way the plastic is layered in the 3D printing process.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One researcher from the 3D printing community even remarked, "they had better chance making a bow and arrow", when asked about those with malicious intent.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At this juncture, I would like to assure everyone that I am not playing down the possibility that on an off-chance, someone might indeed 3D print a weapon and use it for harm.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, while such fears are warranted and everything should be done to curb any instances of such behaviour, it must be asked, are there better ways to do so?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As hon Members, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Melvin Yong had mentioned, not only would it be extremely challenging to monitor the Internet traffic of those with 3D printers, an implausible response time of mere hours, if not minutes, would be required to intervene between the download of a 3D weapon's blueprint to its production.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These same controls on colour copiers were lifted also because of their onerous restrictions, making way for innovation in counterfeit-resistant currency notes in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With the imminent difficulty of enforcement, potential futility of regulation and stifling of a vibrant community with controls on 3D printing, we must consider alternatives.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In this vein, I must inquire, even as we move to enact heavier regulations from above, have we been conscientious to fly low to the ground and explore community alternatives?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: It will harmonise the application of various legislations like the Arms and Explosives Act (AEA), amongst others.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Given that the last review of the Arms and Explosives Act occurred in 2007, this review and introduction of this Bill is timely and welcomed.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Singapore is known for its zero tolerance for the misuse or mishandling of GEWs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Singapore also has one of the most effective gun control legislation in the world; with the number of privately owned firearms remaining relatively constant from 2007 to 2017 and no homicides committed with a gun in recent memory.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: However, now we are faced with newer challenges and different threats to our security and public safety.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Hence, I welcome the changes to tighten the control on high risk GEWs and improve the overall compliance and Police's operational effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this regard, I would like to highlight the refinements which show that the law is also sensitive to the circumstances of each case that an individual may face.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Previously, section 3 of the AOA makes no distinction between possession of arms or ammunition whether with or without criminal intent.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: I welcome such clear distinctions and refinements to the law.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: This may go some way to assuage the concerns of some parents, who are worried of the kind of information that our children may be exposed to on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In this regard, I would humbly suggest, that perhaps MHA could work together with MOE to increase the awareness in schools and our IHLs so that our youth will understand and appreciate the dangers or consequences of having access to such dangerous information.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: My first question, can the Minister clarify the circumstances in which such impracticality will arise?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: My second clarification, I understand that the security direction is given to the person – would this also cover "close associate" of such persons as defined under section 41 or otherwise?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: My third clarification, given that the security direction is non-appealable and that there is no automatic right to be heard under section 64(4).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Would it nevertheless be possible for any aggrieved party to seek judicial review of the process or perhaps, allow a party to seek interim relief for preservation of any asset which may fall under the said security direction.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: (In Malay):    Our world faces various terrorist threats and extremist ideologies that threaten our security.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: We saw how, in 2019, the world was rocked by a shooting case that killed 51 worshippers at a mosque in New Zealand.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Even though our situation in Singapore is very different due to our already very tough laws, we must continue to monitor emerging new threats.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Our world, which is plagued by the COVID-19 outbreaks and economic slowdown, will make more people feel pressured and this may lead to disputes or even domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: On average, trends around the world show that social pressure and social isolation will result in more cases of domestic violence.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: In domestic violence cases in countries such as the United States, Britain and South Africa, nearly 70% of the deaths involve women and the perpetrators are usually their spouses or ex-spouses.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Within these, about one in three murder cases is committed using firearms.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Therefore, we need to continue providing protection to those who are more in need and should not allow any dangerous weapons that can be used to create violence in our society.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: The situation becomes more high-risk because of the unemployment rate and the alienation of workers who face more pressure due to the declining global economy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: Therefore, I agree with the Bill, which will further tighten surveillance and ownership of any details or plans that can be used to produce dangerous weapons through 3D printing technology.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
