text: I welcome the amendments to the Bill that will safeguard our plural society in Singapore and eradicate violence in any form.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim
text: (In English): With that, Mr Speaker, Sir, suggestions and clarifications notwithstanding, I support this Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore is well known for its no nonsense approach to weapons possession.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The possession of guns and firearms by members of the public is prohibited, and the usage of firearms is heavily restricted and generally limited to the armed forces, police and a few private gun clubs.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The possession of other weapons, including items that might be used as weapons such as knives, is also controlled and people are not permitted to be in possession of such items in public without good reason.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Strict laws like this have played an important part in keeping Singapore safe and we do not have horror stories of shootings and gun violence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While we do have other weapons being used in incidents like gang fights, the strict laws against improper possession have also permitted police to move pre-emptively in such cases, arresting individuals in possession of weapons without good reason even if they have not used it for violence yet.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As such, violent fights with weapons are also few and far between.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, these latest changes to legislation and harmonisation of several different Bills tighten and expand the laws to cover developing areas of potential threats.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One example of such a potential threat is the 3D printing of gun parts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While smuggling guns or gun parts into and around Singapore is not easy and subject to the strictest of penalties, it has now become possible to manufacture gun parts with 3D printers, which are becoming more widely available.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The blueprints for such weapons may be found on the Internet, or more commonly, the Dark Net.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With such blueprints and a 3D printer, individuals could 3D print usable gun parts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, this is a tough measure, but one which I welcome as the more easily something dangerous is readily available, the tougher the rules must be to discourage its possession and use.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This sends a clear, no nonsense signal that we are remaining tough on the possession of weapons, even if all that one possesses is a blueprint to 3D print such parts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the use of guns by military and the Police are heavily controlled, one area where members of the public may access weapons is at private shooting ranges.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are some people who participate in lower risk activities such as the use of air rifles for sport.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The introduction of a class licensing regime to deal with these is a clever method and saves each person the hassle of getting an individual licence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Class licences have been used in other areas too, for example, in legislation by MCI in relation to the media, although in this case, given many of the class licensees will be individuals, it will be important for them to know the relevant rules that will apply.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I will be interested to know what steps the Government will take to keep the class licensees informed of such rules.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While the mechanism being used is that of a licence, in substance, what needs to be done is for the individuals in possession of such weapons to know exactly what is permitted and what is not to stay out of trouble.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These are, of course, very sensible and the general principles on which all criminal legislation is based.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There are many questions that have been asked.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I shall address them in turn, first, on the 3D printing of guns, given the strong interest among Members on this topic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Following which, I shall address issues raised by Members thematically.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Many Members raised questions about clause 13 which is on the new offence of unauthorised possession of 3D blueprints for the manufacture of guns or major gun parts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The divergence of views among Members shows that there is no straightforward answer to achieving an appropriate regulatory balance on this matter.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the one hand, Mr Sharael Taha asked if the offence should be widened beyond guns and major gun parts to also cover gun modifications and attachments and offensive weapons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong also took the view that clause 13 should cover possession of digital blueprints for gun replicas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the other hand, Ms Yeo Wan Ling was of the view that 3D printed guns are unlikely to work in practice and that clause 13 could have a chilling effect on innovative applications of 3D printing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill does not change this basic position.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: What the Bill does is to address the new phenomenon where it is increasingly easy for anyone to seek out and acquire online designs and directions on how to make a gun, and using a technology that is increasingly accessible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Major parts of guns are essential to the operation of a gun, such as the barrel or the trigger mechanism and which can be assembled to create a functioning gun.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the other hand, gun accessories are designed to be fitted to or attached to a gun for various purposes, such as to conceal its fire, like a silencer or flash suppressor, or it cannot work except in connection with an operative and functioning gun.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As for weapons like swords and knuckledusters, they are less lethal and dangerous than guns, and therefore, we think there is no necessity at this juncture to also control the possession of 3D blueprints for the manufacture of these weapons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On replica guns, while we agree that they can potentially be used to cause alarm, they cannot be used to cause physical harm per se and therefore similarly pose lower risks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But if such guns are used while committing certain offences, such as robbery and extortion, an offence would be made out under the Arms Offences Act, along with the Penal Code offences for the main criminal act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To address Ms Yeo Wan Ling's point that 3D-printed guns are unlikely to function and her concern on inhibiting innovation, as I mentioned in my Second Reading speech yesterday, the threat posed by the 3D printed guns and gun parts is real.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This point was echoed by other Members as well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There have been genuine cases and online videos demonstrating the use of 3D printed guns or gun parts, especially the metallic ones.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In this regard, we are not alone in addressing this new phenomenon.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, New South Wales also passed laws in 2015 to criminalise the unauthorised possession of 3D blueprint for the manufacturing of firearms.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Licensing the possession of such blueprints will enable the authorities to know who are involved in 3D manufacturing of guns, to ensure that proper security and practices are in place for handling dangerous articles that may potentially be produced as a result.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But I also want to emphasise that items which do not fit the description of a gun under clause 3 of the Bill will not require a licence to possess or 3D print.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 3(4)(c) also makes clear that imitation guns are not considered guns for the purpose of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Therefore, the possession of 3D blueprints for the manufacture of such items will not require a specific licence under clause 13.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the impact on the NERF gun community, off-the-shelf NERF guns are clearly meant for recreational purposes and present little risk, given that the projectiles are foam-based, and are unlikely to cause injury if used properly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Correspondingly, the possession of any blueprint of NERF gun parts will not be regulated.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We will continue to assess how best to apply the right regulatory tools for the various items, in a way that is calibrated to the risks involved, so as not to hamper innovation unnecessarily.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Melvin Yong raised questions pertaining to the enforcement of this offence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Police will enforce in a practical and reasonable manner, based on information that is received, for example, from members of the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In this regard, we agree with Mr Sharael Taha that the community and family members and friends play an important role, such as flagging out potential lone wolves 3D printing guns illegally with intent to cause harm.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Information can be provided to the authorities and will be treated with strict confidence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I also acknowledge at this point Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's point about addressing the underlying motivations behind criminal activity.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Government never loses sight of the need to do so and I thank the Member for his views.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Members also raised questions on the import of guns: how we deal with 3D-printed guns that can escape metal detectors, and the threat of guns and weapon parts imported into Singapore via parcels which are deceptively mislabelled as something else.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Our postal regulations also make it unlawful for a person to send by post or to deliver by post any gun or weapon.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There are robust checks at our checkpoints to detect threat objects, including gun or weapon parts and 3D-printed guns, and Mr Sharael Taha shared an example earlier on.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Incoming parcels are inspected, with the help of technologies other than metal detectors, such as X-ray machines.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Certain persons of interest, such as those flagged up by intelligence agencies to be of security threat, may also be subject to further checks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Enforcement officers at the checkpoints may also conduct random checks, to deter and detect any security threats.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Notwithstanding, we recognise that there is no fool-proof system to fully prevent the import of gun and weapon parts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To complement the already robust measures at the checkpoints, we have a stringent enforcement and regulatory regime inland, as well as severe penalties under the Bill for unlicensed supply, storage and possession of GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This will be a strong deterrence against potential offenders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked for the circumstances under which a person or an organisation would be authorised to possess a 3D blueprint of a gun.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We recognise that there are legitimate reasons to possess digital blueprints of guns in Singapore, such as conducting scientific or law enforcement research.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: And the Bill is not intended to impede such activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Parties that wish to undertake such activities can apply for the appropriate licence or seek special approval from the Minister for Home Affairs under clause 13(2)(c).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They will then have to adhere to licensing or approving conditions, such as, requiring that the blueprints are securely handled and not be left easily accessible by uninvolved persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the questions raised by Mr Sharael Taha on the need to impose export controls on certain types of 3D printers, and by Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Melvin Yong on whether MHA intends to regulate 3D printers, these issues fall beyond the scope of this Bill, which does not deal with 3D printing in itself or 3D printers per se.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I seek the Members' understanding that this will have to be studied in detail, wider, with the relevant agencies and dealt with separately.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Having addressed Members' queries on 3D printing, I will now move on to Members' comments on other clauses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the definition of "store" in clause 2, which is one of the regulated activities covered by the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Paragraphs (c) and (d) in the definition are extensions beyond what would be the exhaustive paragraphs (a) and (b) of the definition of "store".

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They are meant to clarify the situations under which the possession of a certain number of articles or for a certain period for purposes outside of what is in paragraphs (a) and (b) will constitute storage, and not possession, for the purposes of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Otherwise, there is no difference between storing and possession of these items, which has to be regulated differently because of the appreciable risk difference of these activities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To elaborate, if the thresholds are exceeded, the licensee may be required to implement more extensive storage-specific safety and security measures, such as CCTV requirements and hardened walls.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These are over and above the requirements typically placed on licensees who possess a single gun, or handle explosives or explosive precursors for a very short period of time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We acknowledge that with any defined threshold, persons may seek to operate at the margins to avoid taking on additional regulatory burden.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But this is a necessary trade-off between meeting our security objectives and providing stakeholders with clarity on the rules.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To assure this House, regardless of the quantity or duration of possession of such items, a licence will already be required for the possession of these items, setting out basic safety and security conditions that must be adhered to.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: If these quantity or time thresholds need to be revised subsequently due to changes in threat assessment, clause 2(2) of the Bill allows downward adjustments to be made through Regulations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, on the definition of "weapons", Mr Louis Ng also asked if the term is intended to cover imitation, replica or ornamental weapons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The way the Bill has been drafted places only an exhaustive list of actual weapons to be regulated in the First Schedule.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Conversely, "gun" has a broad, descriptive definition in the Bill, and therefore to avoid doubt, the Bill makes clear that imitation and replica guns are excluded.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Notwithstanding, the use of an imitation weapon to threaten or cause fear of injury or death to others would likely be an offence under other Acts, such as the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These items have potential to be misused to cause harm due to their sharp tips or blades.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This would be a light-touch approach that mitigates the risk of misuse of such items, without being overly onerous.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Moving on, I will touch on licensing of shooting range operations and costs to stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We note Mr Derrick Goh’s suggestion to manage the inconvenience and costs to stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I must reiterate that, when designing the regulations and processes, safety and security will remain our topmost priority.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: But within this objective, we are also mindful to minimise regulatory burden as far as possible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Specifically, prior to granting or renewing a shooting range operation licence, there are certain procedures which are fundamental to ensuring the safe conduct of activities that need to be carried out.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: These include inspecting the range premises to ensure the robustness of safety and security measures, and security vetting of key persons.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Where possible, Police have streamlined procedures and processes to make things easier on licensees and applicants.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: For example, Police have digitalised the entire licensing application and renewal process, reducing administrative burden and unnecessary waiting time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, activities such as range time slot booking are managed by the range operators, and are not within the control of the regulator.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the issue of compliance cost, range operators have generally implemented most required measures on their own accord, even today, such as the installation of CCTV systems and setting up access controls into and out of the range premises.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We therefore do not expect the introduction of shooting range licences to impose significant additional costs in the immediate term on these operators.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Next, on class licensing, Mr Derrick Goh asked for assurance that class licensing will not apply to higher risk categories or situations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Vikram also asked about the steps that Government will take to keep class licensees informed of requirements under a class licence.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Relatedly, Mr Louis Ng also asked if variations to class licences will be published in forms more readily accessible to the public, than the Gazette.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To Mr Derrick Goh's question, as class licensing is less stringent than individual licensing from a security standpoint, MHA’s intent is to apply class licensing only to lower-risk activities, such as air gun shooting in school settings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To Mr Vikram's question, under clause 56, class licensing conditions will be published in the Gazette, which is publicly accessible.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Police will also reach out to groups that will be class licensed to make them aware of their regulatory obligations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To Mr Louis Ng's question, the short answer is yes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Variation of class licences will also be published on Police's website; and Police will reach out to affected class licensees, where feasible, to inform them of the changes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the issue of appointment of Compliance Officers raised by Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Louis Ng and Ms Sylvia Lim, to assure this House, Compliance Officers will be required to undergo training and assessment by the Police Licensing Officer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Only qualified Compliance Officers will be authorised to conduct site inspections on behalf of the Licensing Officer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In addition, they will not be allowed to exercise more intrusive enforcement powers such as seizure, search and issuance of composition.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Police Licensing Officer will also conduct audit checks on Compliance Officers to ensure that they are proficient in carrying out their duties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Given these safeguards, and in line with the minimum age for other security-related work such as security officers, MHA has assessed that the minimum age of 18 is appropriate, and there is no need to set a higher minimum age at this juncture.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim raised several questions regarding the security clearance regime, under clauses 43 and 45 of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, on the need to security clear close associates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: While close associates may not handle GEW directly, they need to be security cleared because of the security risk associated with the indirect influence they can exert over the operation of the entity and on the regulated activities the entity conducts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As setting a lower threshold would make it more onerous for businesses, MHA assesses that the 5% threshold is sufficient and balanced, based on the current circumstances.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The threshold can be reviewed from time to time, depending on the threat environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: So, shareholders who hold 5% and above will have to be security cleared.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Second, on whether the Licensing Officer (or LO) has discretion to still grant security clearance if a person fails one or more criteria under clause 45(1).

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The clause does allow the LO to give such weight to the factors, as he considers appropriate, when assessing the security clearance of a person.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Third, on the security clearance for foreigners, such as arms dealers for short-term trade fairs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Police Licensing Officer performs security vetting on all licence applicants, whether foreign or local.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Specifically for foreigners, the Police Licensing Officer will request for relevant documents to show proof that they have been duly licensed or authorised by the source countries to handle the GEW.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: To further mitigate the security risks associated with imported guns and explosives, all movement of such high-risk items in Singapore must be escorted and guarded by armed auxiliary police officers, thereby minimising the chances of the items being misused or mishandled.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Zhulkarnian asked about security directions under clause 64.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: First, on the circumstances for which security direction may be issued.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: As mentioned in my earlier speech, security directions issued by Minister can be used where there is imminent threat to life or property.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A possible scenario is where there is an on-going suspected terrorist incident, such that for public safety reasons, licensees and even those who are exempted from holding GEW licences must immediately enhance their security posture or completely shut their premises for a specified period to prevent the terrorists from getting their hands on guns and explosives.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In such a scenario, issuing a security direction would be critical to mitigate the threat first, given that the matter is of such urgency and magnitude that there is not enough time for regulations to be amended or new regulations to be made, and for the due process under clause 63 or licence conditions to be modified.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: A security direction can only apply to a licensee, class licensee or person exempted from the Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: They are ultimately responsible for the regulated activity and are best placed to take necessary action to comply with the security direction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: It would be ineffective and disproportionate for a security direction to apply also to a close associate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: On the need for asset preservation, the Member need not be concerned because the security direction is aimed at dealing with a particular situation and is valid only for a period of up to six months.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Asset disposal or destruction will not be an appropriate response in a security direction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: I will now progress to other issues raised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Using imitation guns to commit certain scheduled offences such as robbery and extortion continues to be a serious offence under the Arms Offences Act.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The offender can be jailed for up to 10 years and be liable for caning of no fewer than three strokes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: In the past, the Police used to issue gun possession licence to private individuals, such as arms dealers, for self-protection; but this is no longer practised today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked on the defences and counter measures against drone attacks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Clause 97 updates the reference in the Air Navigation Act to refer to this new Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: We have developed some capabilities, and are testing more methods to counter drones used for illicit purposes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, I will not be able to share more due to the sensitivity of the operations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Lastly, Mr Zhulkarnain and Mr Gan Thiam Poh raised the concern of access to harmful online content relating to GEW, terrorism and other materials.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: However, preventing terrorism use of GEW is but one aspect of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: There are more specific and focused laws like the Terrorism (Suppression of Bombings) Act and the United Nations (Anti-terrorism Measures) Regulations to address the threat of terrorism.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: This Bill works alongside other laws to keep the threat of online harms at bay.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: That said, the threat of online influence lies outside of this scope and Members may consider filing specific parliamentary questions for this to be addressed holistically.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: The Bill is a crucial piece of legislation that will go a long way to continue to ensure safe, secure and responsible GEW handling in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Home Affairs (Mr Desmond Tan)
text: Once again, I thank Members for their strong support for this Bill.
